li.a: Ynetnews (AFP): Kozo Okamoto's long life after Israel suicide mission 50 years ago
Jewish Currents: The Lod Airport Terrorist Attack
United States District Court for the District of Puerto Rico: Calderon-Cardona v. Democratic People's Republic of Korea, opinion and order, 16 July 2010
Rewards For Justice: Attack on Lod Airport (May 30, 1972)
JNS: Japanese terrorist behind 1972 Lod Airport massacre dies

content.p: On 30 May 1972, passengers stepping off a flight from Rome into the arrivals hall of Lod Airport, near Tel Aviv, collected their bags from the carousel. Three of them were carrying weapons. When the shooting ended, 26 people were dead and, by the count of a United States federal court, more than 80 wounded. The gunmen were Japanese, members of the Japanese Red Army, and they were working with a Palestinian organisation, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which trained them and helped plan the operation, according to the United States government's Rewards for Justice programme.

Only eight of the dead were Israelis. Seventeen were Christian pilgrims from Puerto Rico on a trip to the Holy Land, and one was a Canadian. The one attacker who survived, Kozo Okamoto, went before an Israeli military tribunal, received a life sentence, was freed after 13 years in a prisoner exchange, and lived his later years in Lebanon, where he was reported dead in July 2026.
content.h2: An attack from inside the arrivals hall
content.p: A United States federal judge, hearing a lawsuit by relatives of victims, set out the events as the plaintiffs' evidence established them. The three attackers had disguised themselves as ordinary passengers. They had just arrived on a flight from Italy. Out of their bags came automatic weapons and grenades, and the firing and grenade-throwing into the crowded terminal began.

Jewish Currents, in an anniversary note, described the attackers as dressed conservatively and carrying violin cases from which they drew sawed-off assault rifles. AFP reporting published by Ynetnews added that earlier PFLP hijackings had already led airlines to screen passengers more tightly, but that checks of luggage in the hold were still uncommon. The three men passed immigration without trouble.

The court heard from Ze'ev Sarig, who in 1972 was an assistant to the deputy director of the airport and later became its managing director. According to the opinion, no armed Israeli security personnel were stationed inside the terminal that day, so the attackers met no organised resistance. Sarig testified that no attack launched from inside an airport by people arriving on an incoming flight had happened before, which is why security had not planned for one.

Two of the three attackers died during the assault. The accounts differ on how. The American court recorded that one was struck by a ricocheting bullet and the other by a grenade that went off too early. Rewards for Justice said two members of the group were killed by security personnel. JNS named the two dead men as Tsuyoshi Okudaira and Yasuyuki Yasuda.

According to the court, the third man, Okamoto, ran out of the terminal intending to blow up aircraft on the tarmac. An airport employee, Claude Chanan Zeitoun, unarmed, chased him near the runway, knocked the rifle away and held him until police arrived. Rewards for Justice and JNS say instead that Okamoto was wounded and arrested. AFP, reporting through Ynetnews, wrote that the plan was a suicide attack and that all three had meant to disfigure their own faces with grenades to hinder identification.

The toll of 26 appears in most of the sources opened here; a brief 2026 Ynetnews obituary says Okamoto murdered 24, a figure that sits unexplained against the others. The court counted over 80 wounded; JNS gave 80. The dead were 17 Puerto Rican pilgrims, a Canadian and eight Israelis, according to AFP and JNS.

The court's opinion put faces on a few of them. Carmelo Calderon-Molina and Pablo Tirado-Ayala were part of a large group on a church-organised pilgrimage, which the court described as a trip many participants had saved for over years. Calderon-Molina was killed; the court's findings say his last act was to shield a pregnant woman with his body, and his daughter Gloria testified that the survivor later came to thank the family. She came with her husband to the family's home to thank them. He left a widow and ten children. Tirado-Ayala was wounded and, the court found, suffered severe psychological injuries for the rest of his life. He died on 29 December 2009 for reasons the court said were unrelated to the attack.
The court also recorded the death of Adam Tzamir, aged 11, who had gone with his parents to meet a relative and was killed in the arrivals hall.

Among the Israeli dead was Aharon Katzir, a protein biophysicist who headed the Israeli National Academy of Sciences. JNS wrote that he was a likely front-runner in the coming Israeli presidential election. Ephraim Katzir, his brother, won the presidency a year later. In Puerto Rico, AFP noted, a remembrance ceremony is still held every 30 May in San Juan.

Japanese attackers had a practical use to the Palestinian side. The court heard from Sarig, and from the expert Professor Barry Rubin, that the PFLP knew Japanese nationals would not draw the scrutiny Israeli security gave Arabs travelling from Lebanon.

The judgment records a chain of introductions. According to the opinion's account of Okamoto's own recollections, his brother Takashi, one of the men who had hijacked a Japanese airliner to North Korea in March 1970, brought him into the Japanese Red Army. Takashi, based in Pyongyang, sent him to Beirut in September 1971 for a seven-week training course with the PFLP. At its end he was told he had been picked for the Lod operation.

According to the opinion, Okamoto admitted under interrogation that the attackers were Japanese Red Army members and that the attack had been carried out together with the PFLP. The PFLP publicly claimed responsibility, a claim widely reported in the international press, the court noted. The Rewards for Justice page describes the Japanese Red Army as a group formed around 1970, whose stated aim was to overthrow the Japanese government and monarchy. Among the group's other attacks it counts an attempt to take over the US embassy in Kuala Lumpur in 1975 and a bombing at a USO club in Naples in 1988.

Jewish Currents named Wadie Haddad, whom it called the primary organiser of the attack and later the organiser of the Entebbe airport operation, and said he was poisoned to death by Mossad in early 1978. It added that a senior KGB defector later told British intelligence Haddad had been a Soviet recruit. Those are the magazine's statements; none of the other pages opened here mention them.

Okamoto faced an Israeli military tribunal. Rewards for Justice says it found him guilty and sentenced him to life imprisonment in June 1972. AFP described how he had tried to get the death penalty. According to the AFP account, he had allegedly struck a deal with an Israeli general in custody, in which he would give information in exchange for a weapon to kill himself, and was tricked out of his side of it. His court-appointed Israeli lawyer was quoted, from a 1976 interview by the academic Patricia Steinhoff, as saying Okamoto was "working for the prosecution". Israel had carried out the death penalty only once, against the Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann, AFP noted. Okamoto got life instead.
Jewish Currents quoted him as telling the Japanese embassy that he had done his "duty as a soldier of the revolution".

In May 1985 Okamoto was freed in a large prisoner exchange. The sources give the exchange differently. Rewards for Justice says he went free with more than 1,100 other prisoners in return for two Israeli soldiers held by Palestinian militant factions. JNS says Israel released 1,150 prisoners under the Jibril Agreement with the PFLP General Command, in exchange for three Israelis captured in the 1982 war in Lebanon. Jewish Currents says more than 1,000 prisoners were released and that he served 13 years.

AFP described him on his release as barely alive. A photograph taken at Tripoli airport in Libya showed Palestinian fighters hoisting him on their shoulders while his eyes were glazed. A PFLP official in Beirut, Abu Yusef, said he looked "like a corpse". The PFLP's account, which AFP reported without independent confirmation, was that he had spent much of his time in Israeli jail in solitary confinement, with his hands cuffed behind his back.

Rewards for Justice says he lived in Libya and Syria before moving to Lebanon. AFP wrote that after years in Japanese Red Army camps in the Bekaa Valley he was arrested in 1997 on forgery charges. In 2000, under pressure from Tokyo, Lebanon extradited four other members of the group; Okamoto was released and granted asylum after weeks of pro-Palestinian demonstrations. AFP called him Lebanon's first and only political refugee. May Shigenobu, the daughter of the Japanese Red Army's founder, told AFP that Japan was still asking for his extradition every year.

In May 2022, at the 50th anniversary, he came out of seclusion for a rare appearance. PFLP militants escorted him to a cemetery on the edge of the Shatila camp in Beirut, where he laid a wreath for the two comrades who died in the attack, smiled for cameras and made a V-sign, AFP reported. It described a quiet life in semi-hiding: meals at set times, hours of cartoons on television and, at 74, a recent end to smoking. May Shigenobu, daughter of the Japanese Red Army founder Fusako Shigenobu, said at the time that he was no threat to Israel or Japan.
JNS reported in July 2026, citing reports published that Thursday, that Okamoto had died in Beirut at 78; it attributed its account of his life in Lebanon to the PFLP.
content.h2: North Korea in a Puerto Rican courtroom
content.p: In 2008 the families of two Puerto Rican victims filed suit in the federal court in San Juan under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act. The defendants were North Korea and its Cabinet General Intelligence Bureau. The plaintiffs alleged the attack was a joint Japanese Red Army and PFLP operation backed by North Korean material support. The defendants did not appear, and the case went forward as a motion for default judgment, with an evidentiary hearing on 2 and 3 December 2009.

The plaintiffs relied chiefly on three expert witnesses, Barry Rubin, Bruce Bechtol and Rohan Gunaratna, and on two eyewitnesses, Sarig and Zeitoun. Their evidence, as the judge summarised it, was that North Korea sheltered the Japanese Red Army's leadership, trained its members or arranged their training, and provided funds and weapons. According to the evidence the court summarised, the PFLP leader George Habash visited Pyongyang in September 1970, met the Japanese group's leadership, including Okamoto's brother, and asked the group to supply operatives for the Lod attack. Rubin also testified that the group chose operatives who had not lived in North Korea so that Pyongyang could deny involvement. Gunaratna testified that North Korean instructors trained Japanese Red Army members in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley.

On 16 July 2010, Judge Francisco Besosa ruled that the plaintiffs had shown by clear and convincing evidence that North Korea and the bureau were jointly and severally liable for providing material support to the attackers. The awards included $15 million for the estate of the wounded Tirado-Ayala, $8 million for the estate of Calderon-Molina's widow, $5 million to each of several of his children, and $10 million to Tirado-Ayala's wife, Antonia. The court added punitive damages of $300 million, to be divided among the plaintiffs, noting that North Korea's budget for exporting terrorism was not known and adopting the figure courts had typically used against Iran. This was a default judgment on the plaintiffs' evidence, with no defence heard from North Korea.

The Rewards for Justice programme still offers up to $5 million for information on those responsible for the attack. It notes that the United States designated the Japanese Red Army a foreign terrorist organisation in October 1997 and revoked the designation in October 2001 after the group disbanded. The airport where it happened was renamed Ben Gurion International in 1973, according to JNS.
